paragraphs: Money from Ireland's TV licence went down by €5.7 million in the first nine months of 2026, new numbers show. By the end of September, people bought just over 536,500 licences. That is about 35,700 fewer than last year, or 6 per cent less.

A licence costs €160, and An Post collects the money. About 85 per cent of it goes to RTÉ, the national TV and radio company. Small parts go to the media watchdog and to An Post for its work. For the whole year, the licence will bring in about €114 million. In 2022, it brought in almost €152 million.

There are a few reasons for the drop. In 2023 there was a big problem about secret payments at RTÉ. Also, more homes now have no TV. And the population is getting older, so every year more homes can get a free licence.

Aidan Farrelly, a TD from the Social Democrats, said the system is not just broken but has fallen apart. He wants big changes. Media Minister Patrick O'Donovan has a report from a group of experts about ways to pay for public media, and he will show it to the Government soon. RTÉ said it is very important to know clearly how public media will get money.

Income from Ireland's television licence fell by €5.7 million in the first nine months of 2026, new figures show. Just over 536,500 licences were sold by the end of September, about 35,700 fewer than a year earlier, a drop of 6 per cent.

The licence costs €160 and is collected by An Post. Around 85 per cent of the money goes to the national broadcaster RTÉ, while smaller shares go to the media regulator and to An Post for collecting it. For the full year, income is expected to be about €114 million, compared with nearly €152 million in 2022.

The fall has several causes: the payments controversy at RTÉ in 2023, a growing number of homes without a television, and an ageing population, since more households qualify for a free licence every year.

Social Democrats TD Aidan Farrelly said the system had not just broken but collapsed, and called for full reform. Media Minister Patrick O'Donovan has received a report from a working group on funding options and plans to bring it to Government soon. RTÉ said clear funding for public service media is vital.

Revenue from Ireland's television licence slid by €5.7 million in the first nine months of 2026, newly released figures reveal. Slightly more than 536,500 licences had been sold by the end of September, roughly 35,700 fewer than a year earlier, a decline of 6 per cent.

The €160 levy is collected by An Post. Approximately 85 per cent of the proceeds flow to the national broadcaster RTÉ, with smaller portions going to the media regulator and to An Post for its collection work. Full-year receipts are forecast at around €114 million, a far cry from the almost €152 million raised in 2022.

The slump stems from a combination of factors: the 2023 payments scandal at RTÉ, a mounting number of television-free homes, and an ageing population, as ever more households become eligible for a free licence each year.

Social Democrats TD Aidan Farrelly declared that the system had gone beyond being broken and had in fact collapsed, demanding a wholesale overhaul. Media Minister Patrick O'Donovan has received a report from a working group examining funding options and intends to bring it before Government shortly. RTÉ stressed that clarity over the funding of public service media is vital.
